summary: Defines a new authentication method for the Authentication-Results header field, defined in RFC 7001, to report the results of S/MIME signature checks.

plainLanguage.summary: When an email is signed, the mail system can write a note on it saying whether the signature was checked. This adds a note type for it.

subtitle: Reporting S/MIME signature verification results in email headers

tldr.problem: Email systems sometimes verify S/MIME signatures on messages, but have no standard way to report whether the verification succeeded or failed to downstream mail user agents.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7281 registers a new 'smime' authentication method for the Authentication-Results header field, allowing mail systems to report seven result codes indicating the outcome of signature verification.
tldr.outcome: Mail user agents can now receive standardized signature verification results without verifying signatures themselves, though they should ideally do their own verification when possible.

facts.label: Result codes
facts.value: none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror, permerror

today: RFC 7281 is an Informational RFC that remains active and has not been obsoleted. It is used by mail systems that perform S/MIME verification to report results to downstream mail user agents.

sections.title: Adding S/MIME to Authentication-Results
sections.content:
RFC 7001 defines the Authentication-Results header field, which allows email systems to report the results of authentication checks such as SPF and DKIM. This RFC extends that framework to cover S/MIME signature verification, where a mail transfer agent, gateway, or filter verifies that a message was cryptographically signed and that the signature is valid.

S/MIME verification happens in border systems (security appliances at network edges) that sit between senders and recipients. When these systems check signatures, they need a way to tell downstream mail user agents what they found, without the agents having to re-verify the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Some email systems check if a message is really from who it says. Now they can tell other systems what they found using a standard format instead of each system checking from scratch.

sections.title: S/MIME Result Codes
sections.content:
The 'smime' authentication method uses seven result codes to report verification outcomes. A result of none means the message was not signed. A pass result means the message was signed, the signature was acceptable per local policy checks, and verification succeeded. A fail result means the signature failed the verification test, and policy means the signature passed verification but failed local policy (such as a certificate being revoked). The code neutral indicates syntax errors or other unspecified processing failures. The codes temperror and permerror distinguish temporary problems (like a missing certificate that might be available later) from permanent ones (like a required header missing).

The RFC notes that a verifier may require that the sender's domain matches the domain in the signing certificate's rfc822Name subjectAltName, making third-party signatures unacceptable. If verification fails, the RFC advises treating the message as unsigned rather than reporting it as signed with a bad signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The result codes are: the message wasn't signed (none), the signature is good (pass), the signature is bad (fail), the signature is good but not allowed (policy), the signature has errors (neutral), we couldn't check it now but might later (temperror), or we can never check it (permerror).

sections.title: S/MIME Authentication Parameters
sections.content: The RFC defines four new authentication parameters that can accompany the 'smime' result. The body.smime-part parameter specifies which MIME body part contains the signature, using IMAP section syntax that can reference nested MIME parts in encrypted structures. The body.smime-identifier parameter contains the email address associated with the signature, taken from either the signer's certificate or the certificate subject. The body.smime-serial parameter holds the serial number of the X.509 certificate, and body.smime-issuer contains the certificate's issuer distinguished name (DN). The serial and issuer parameters are used when the email address cannot be extracted, such as when gatewaying from X.400.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameters say where the signature is in the message, who signed it, and certificate details if needed. They're like address labels on the signed part of the message.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers the 'smime' method in IANA's Email Authentication Methods registry, along with the four parameters and all seven result codes. Each registration is marked active and references RFC 7281 as the defining source. This centralized registration ensures that all implementations use the same terminology and prevent collisions with other authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard names and result codes are officially recorded so everyone uses the same words.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: The RFC defers its security considerations to RFC 7001 and RFC 5751, the base standards for Authentication-Results and S/MIME. The key warning from RFC 7001 is that a mail user agent or filter reading Authentication-Results header fields from a non-conformant mail transfer agent could draw false conclusions if a malicious user forged the header. For this reason, applications should not enable Authentication-Results processing by default; it should be ignored for filtering decisions unless the user or administrator explicitly enables it after verifying that the border MTA is compliant. An MUA may maintain an explicit list of trusted authentication sources, though this list should start empty. Most importantly, whenever possible, mail user agents should implement their own S/MIME signature verification rather than relying on this header alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't trust the header unless you trust whoever added it. It's better if your email program checks signatures itself rather than trusting what a gateway wrote.
